en: The Sūtra on the Measurement of Lifespans Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated at the Mi-lin Monastery in Jālandhara, Central India,
by the Tripitaka Master Mingjiao, who was bestowed with the purple robe.
Translated by the śramaṇa subject Tianxi'ai by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively as I compare the lengths of the lifespans of sentient beings.
The bhikṣus replied: [We shall do so.]
“World-Honored One!
We would delight to hear it.
At that time, the Sugata explained to the bhikṣus matters such as the comparative measurements of the lifespans of sentient beings.
When the assembly of bhikṣus heard these words, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound it."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You should listen attentively; I shall now speak for you.”
In the Avīci Hell, the lifespan lasts for the remainder of an intermediate kalpa; the lifespans in the seven higher hells vary in length and duration.
Bhikṣus, you should know that these are the measurements of kalpas for the lifespans in the hells, and only after the suffering has been fully experienced does one’s life come to an end.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that thirty days and nights among human beings constitute one day and night in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
Thirty such days and nights form one month for them; twelve such months form one year for them. By this reckoning of years, five hundred years is the full lifespan in the realm of hungry ghosts.”

If one were to calculate by comparison across the four great continents, the lifespan in the northern continent is one thousand years; in the western and eastern continents, it is successively reduced by half; and in the southern continent, it is indefinite—it was immeasurable at the beginning of the kalpa, ten years at its end, and variable in between.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Constantly tormented by the *saṃghāta* hell, their lips and throats parched by the retribution of their karma;
the hairs on their bodies all stand on end, and their bellies are as vast as mountains.”
Their hair is disheveled, constantly covering their bodies; their needle-like mouths are as fine as blade-edges.
Their faces and eyes are all cleft and torn; emaciated by hunger, their skeletal forms are exposed.
Crimson hair covers their own bodies, and their joints and bones are laid bare.
Drinking from the skulls of the wicked necks, they constantly run about wailing.
They suffer the torments of hunger and thirst; exhausted and perpetually oppressed, their cries of bitter lamentation ring out loud. What one has done oneself, one must experience for oneself.
Greed and hatred arise from the encounter with the agreeable and disagreeable;
having created the causes of evil karma for oneself, when these karmic obstacles of sin ripen, one undergoes rebirth within the realm of hungry ghosts.
For the people of Pūrvavideha, the lifespan is two hundred and fifty years.
In Aparagoyānī, the lifespan is five hundred years;
Born in Uttarakuru, the lifespan is fixed at one thousand years;
In Jambudvīpa, the lifespan is not fixed: At the end it is ten years, and at the beginning it is immeasurable.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that those in Uttarakuru have a lifespan of one thousand years before their lives come to an end?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should know that in Uttarakuru, there is no grasping at a self and no conceptual discrimination. Because they practice the ten wholesome paths of action, their lifespan is fixed at one thousand years; when their lives end here, they are reborn in the heavens."
"In this way, those in Uttarakuru have a lifespan of one thousand years, after which they pass away.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Poor sentient beings, suffering, Covetously steal the wealth and property of others."
Those who have never cultivated wholesome deeds are lowly and base, driven by others;
those who possess great wealth and nobility, with all the necessities of life fully provided—
gold, jade, and servants— it is such people who perform wholesome deeds.
By cultivating the causes of the ten virtuous actions, one attains the fruit of great wealth and nobility;
in the present life one experiences the continent of Uttarakuru, and thereafter is born in the heavens in happiness.
The people of the continent of Uttarakuru enjoy the greatest pleasure in the world.
In the past, they cultivated the cause of generosity; the fruit is the wondrous garments of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
They have no suffering from cold or heat, nor do they have any afflictions of disease.
Their physical forms are wondrously dignified and handsome—this is because in the past they cultivated the cause of generosity.
Merit is supreme and difficult to destroy; Rice grows spontaneously, pure and brilliant white— This is due to having practiced generosity in the past.
Born in Uttarakuru, The mani-jewels shine with radiance.
Food and drink are accomplished through thought; this was due to practicing generosity in the past.
That continent is most peaceful and blissful; excellent medicines are always abundant there.
It is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor; this was due to practicing generosity in the past.
On that continent there are no vegetables; they constantly eat fragrant rice.
Once received, the food is inexhaustible, due to having practiced generosity in the past.
At the āmalaka fruit tree, he eats while remaining seated without rising.
Branches fall and fruits grow anew because of past cultivation of giving;
That water possesses the eight qualities, for when drunk it causes no illness or distress,
bringing peace and comfort without harming the belly, because of past cultivation of giving.
One experiences joy in gardens and groves, Constantly hears sublime sounds,
And finds perpetual, inexhaustible delight— These result from practicing generosity in the past.
The kalpavṛkṣa tree is loved by all, It rains down pleasant ointments and perfumes;
The fragrance of the wind is inexhaustible, due to having practiced giving in the past;
Music, exquisite flowers and incense, clothing, and ornaments for the body—
these appear according to one's thoughts, due to having practiced giving in the past.
The fragrant herbs and mountain groves are all soft and vast;
they always delight in playing there because in the past they practiced giving.
They constantly enjoy such pleasures together, for anger never arises within them.
Selfless and free from craving, this is due to practicing generosity in the past;
Each night at the first watch, a fine drizzle falls gently,
Dust is removed and the ground is pure, this is due to practicing generosity in the past.
The son grows up without knowing his mother; when her life ends, she has no grief.
She has severed the heart of craving and attachment because, in the past, she practiced giving.
A compassionate mother gives birth to an infant, yet on the road, she abandons him and departs.
The milk flows and gushes from his fingers—this is due to practicing generosity in the past;
At the time of death, he abandons everything, yet feels not the slightest bit of grief or lamentation—this is due to practicing generosity in the past;
Birds carry him away to a pure land—this is due to practicing generosity in the past.
Magnificent adornments cover everywhere;
with song and dance, all enjoy playful delights, finding contentment and happiness—this is due to having practiced generosity in the past.
The lifespan of the people on that continent is fully one thousand years.
They shall never suffer premature death, for they cultivated generosity in the past;
their merit is most supreme and equal without distinction,
and at the end of life they will be reborn in heaven, for they cultivated generosity in the past.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The lifespan in this Jambudvīpa is not fixed; it begins from ten years and extends up to a hundred thousand million years, with lifespans being immeasurable."
"Monks, you should know that the lifespan of people in Jambudvīpa today is one hundred years, with many dying prematurely and no fixed duration.
Monks, you should know that although the people of Jambudvīpa have a long life of one hundred years, suffering is much and happiness is little."
"Furthermore, monks! Although the lifespan in this continent is one hundred years, it is divided into ten stages:

first, *vālu*, being unaware while lying in sleep; second, *kumāru*, engaging in play and beginning to understand life; third, *yauvana*, being attached to the objects of desire; fourth, *marabhaṅga*, diligently applying oneself to one's work; fifth, *prājñā*, possessing exceptional wisdom and eloquence; sixth, *smṛtimat*, being clear-headed and retentive; seventh, *sthavira*, properly establishing oneself in right conduct; eighth, *vīra*, being protected with compassion by the king; ninth, *mṛtyu*, when the complexion fades and strength diminishes; and tenth, *nirjīva*, reaching the end of life after several hundred years."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!
Before the hundred years have ended, there are three seasons: namely, cold, heat, and rain; these are also called the three times."
Before the hundred years have ended, within those twelve months, one obtains the designation of the three seasons:
four months of the cold season, four months of the hot season, and four months of the rainy season.
Furthermore, within those twelve months before the hundred years have ended, there are twenty-four half-months.
Before the hundred years have ended, within them there are eight months of the cold season, eight months of the hot season, and eight months of the rainy season.

Furthermore, within the twelve months of a hundred-year span, there are thirty-six days and nights; within each month, there are twelve periods of the cold season, twelve periods of the hot season, and twelve periods of the rainy season.

Furthermore, within a thousand years, there are thirty-six months of twenty-four-hour days; during this period, there are seventy-two thousand instances of eating. Among these, there are times when one eats and times when one does not eat—namely, when one is angry, when one is afflicted by suffering, when traveling on a road, when observing a fast, when preoccupied with urgent business, when sleeping, and when intoxicated or dazed;

in all such cases, one does not eat. Moreover, there are instances where food is obtained but not eaten, and instances where food is neither obtained nor eaten. Such instances of eating and non-eating—briefly speaking, regarding those occasions when food is obtained—amount to seventy-two thousand times of eating.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

Regarding this Jambudvīpa as previously described, and from the time of being nursed by the wet-nurse, through the months, fortnights, days and nights, and years—this is spoken with reference to the interval between the times of eating and the times of not eating."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I have said that a human lifespan of fifty years constitutes one day and night in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Thirty such days and nights constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year. With a lifespan of five hundred such years, when calculated in terms of human days and nights, their life spans amount to nine million (ninety lakṣas), after which they pass away."

Five hundred years of the lifespan in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell; thirty such days and nights constitute one month there, and twelve such months constitute one year there. By this reckoning of years, five hundred years is the lifespan of sentient beings within the great Saṃjīva Hell.

Those five hundred years correspond to five hundred and forty lakṣas in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; when calculated by human reckoning, this equals sixteen thousand two hundred koṭis of years, at which point the lifespan in the Saṃjīva Great Hell is finally exhausted.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Evil karma of the body consists of three types; Karma of the mouth consists of four evils;
The three karmas of the mind are likewise so. Only when the retribution for these sins is exhausted does one finally emerge from suffering."
Within the Saṃjīva Hell, those with identical evil karma all enter;
for sixteen hundred and twenty koṭis of years, they constantly endure suffering.
Born within that hell, enemies slaughter one another.
"Having died, they revive once more; only when their karma is exhausted does suffering finally end.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"One hundred years among humans constitute one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Thirty such days and nights constitute one month there, and twelve such months constitute one year. The lifespan in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is one thousand years."
"By comparison with the reckoning of human years, one thousand years in that heaven equals eighteen *koṭis* of years;
thereafter, those beings in that heaven pass away. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"One thousand years of the lifespan in that heaven constitutes a single day and night in the Black Rope (*Kālasūtra*) Great Hell. Thirty such days and nights constitute a month and a year. The lifespan in that Great Hell is one thousand such years; by calculation, this one thousand-year period corresponds to thirty-two thousand four hundred *koṭis* of human years, after which those beings in the Black Rope Great Hell finally pass away."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Hating and despising one's teacher and parents, Slandering the Buddha and the śrāvakas,
And destroying those who promote harmony— One shall undergo great suffering in the Kālasūtra Hell."
"Having personally committed evil karma, one must undergo the suffering of hell;
there is no way to avoid it, for only when the karma is exhausted does one finally emerge.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Two hundred human years constitute one day and night for the Yāma gods. Thirty such days and nights form a month, and twelve such months form a year. The lifespan of those Yāma gods is two thousand of their own years; by human calculation, this amounts to thirty-six koṭis of years when measured as a lifespan, after which they finally pass away."

Furthermore, two thousand years of the lifespan of those devas constitutes one day and night in the Saṃghāta Great Hell; thirty such days and nights constitute one month there, and twelve such months constitute one year there. The lifespan in that Saṃghāta Great Hell is two thousand such years; when calculated by human reckoning, it corresponds to sixty-four thousand eight hundred *koṭis* of years, after which those beings finally pass away from that hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By committing three kinds of unwholesome karma, One is born in the Saṃghāta Hell;
Failing to cultivate the three wholesome karmas, One suffers as an ox, a sheep, or a deer, being subjected to slaughter."
"Pigs, dogs, and non-humans, gathered together, kill one another;
born from the cause of suffering in a place of suffering, they only emerge once their karma is exhausted.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Four hundred human years constitute one day and night for the Tuṣita Heaven. Thirty such days and nights form a month and a year there; the lifespan of those in the Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand celestial years, which, when calculated by human reckoning, amounts to seventy-two koṭis of years. Only after that span of life does their existence in that heaven come to an end."

Four thousand years in that heaven constitute one day and night in the Great Hell of Screaming (Raurava). Thirty such days and nights form a month and a year; thus, the lifespan in the Great Hell of Screaming is four thousand years, which corresponds to four thousand three hundred and twenty *koṭis* of years in the Tuṣita Heaven, and twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand *koṭis* of years in the human realm. Only after this duration does one’s life in the Great Hell of Screaming come to an end.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Committing the ultimate evil of killing, One constantly undergoes the retribution of wailing.
For those who perform evil and deceive others, Only when their karma is exhausted does suffering finally end."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for the gods who Delight in Emanation (Nirmāṇarati). Thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. By this calculation, the lifespan of the gods who Delight in Emanation is eight thousand celestial years; compared to the human reckoning, this amounts to one hundred forty-four koṭis of years, after which their life there comes to an end."

Furthermore, since the lifespan of those gods is eight thousand years, this constitutes a single day and night in the Great Howling (Mahāraurava) great hell. Calculating thirty such days and nights as one month and twelve months as one year, the lifespan in that Great Howling great hell—eight thousand years by their reckoning—is equivalent to twenty-five hundred and ninety thousand *koṭis* of human years when measured; only after that duration does their life come to an end.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The view of self and lustful desire, The sin of slandering the Dharma is most profound;
Committing evil and being bound by the hindrances— One is born amidst the Great Screaming Hell."
In the Great Hell of Screaming, the hairs on one's body all stand erect;
Devouring and drinking flames that burn, one turns away but finds no escape from the prohibitions.
Through falsehood and the love of killing, there are sword-wheels, dogs, herons, and birds.
"The old iron crows devour the marrow; none can escape their cruel slaughter.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"One thousand six hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods. Thirty such days and nights constitute a month, and twelve months constitute a year. By this calculation, the lifespan of those Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods is sixteen thousand years, which by human reckoning equals two hundred and eighty-eight koṭis of years. Only after that period does their life come to an end."

Furthermore, sixteen thousand years in that heaven constitute one day and night in the Great Hell of Intense Heat (Tapana). Thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year. The lifespan in that Great Hell of Intense Heat is sixteen thousand years; when calculated by human reckoning, this corresponds to six million eight hundred and forty quadrillion (*koṭi*) years, after which one’s life in that hell finally comes to an end.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who harass their parents, Śramaṇas, and Brāhmaṇas,
Failing to cultivate wholesome deeds, Constantly undergo the suffering of the Fiery Heat."
"Deceiving and deluding all sentient beings, they shall suffer in the Reviving (Saṃjīva) and the Heating (Tapana) hells;
the evil they have committed does not perish, and only when their karma is exhausted will they finally emerge from here.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“You should listen attentively as I calculate and enumerate the lifespans of sentient beings in the Arbuda hell and the other hells.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Well-gone One!”
“We would delight to hear, receive, and remember this; we only pray that you will explain the comparison of the lengths of life for sentient beings in the Blister Hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
I shall now, for your sake, explain in detail the matter of the lifespan in this Blistering Hell (Arbuda).

Suppose a single *vāha* measure were filled with sesame seeds, capable of holding twenty *khārī*; if a celestial being were to remove one seed every hundred years until all twenty *khārī* were exhausted, only then would the lifespan in that Blistering Hell be completed.

"Furthermore, monks, I shall explain the measurement of the lifespans of sentient beings. For example, as in the *Bubbulaka* hell, the lifespan is twenty *vāha* of sesame seeds; likewise, in the *Ataṭa* hell, the lifespan is forty *vāha* of sesame seeds; in the *Hahava* hell, it is sixty *vāha* of sesame seeds; in the *Huhuva* hell, it is eighty *vāha* of sesame seeds; in the *Utpala* hell, it is one hundred *vāha* of sesame seeds; in the *Padma* hell, it is one hundred and twenty *vāha* of sesame seeds; and thus, in the *Mahāpadma* hell, the lifespan is one hundred and forty *vāha* of sesame seeds. In each of these hells, there is a full basket of sesame seeds from which one seed is removed every hundred years; only when every single seed has been exhausted does the lifespan of those sentient beings come to an end."
“Thus it is, bhikṣus!
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Devadatta, and their respective retinues—if there be another person whose mental conduct is violent and evil, that person shall themselves fall into this great hell.”
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should understand it thus:
if there is another person whose body is afflicted by emaciation, one should not give rise to anger toward them nor feel contempt in one's mind. Therefore, bhikṣus!
"The wise person should thus cultivate awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person utters evil words, Destroying others like a blade or an axe,"
A wheel of swords shall sever his body, all emerging from his own mouth;
having slandered the virtuous and good, yet praising them with delight,
and having bound himself in strife and enmity, he enters hell swiftly upon death.
When one covets the wealth belonging to others, giving rise to jealousy through strife,
and causes them distress and lack of peace, one shall suffer the agony of the Bursting Ulcer Hell.
If one slanders the Sugata with a mind that finds delight and joy [in such malice], [one shall likewise suffer].
For hundreds of thousands of *vibhūṣaṇa* kalpas, one will constantly suffer the pains of hell.
Having given rise to evil in body, speech, and mind, and having slandered the various noble sages—
five hundred and thirty-six times— one will constantly suffer during the *vibhūṣaṇa* kalpas.
"Having extensively committed boundless deeds—offenses and falsehoods—one remains within the hells for long eons;
only after that karma is exhausted does one finally emerge.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“In this Great Hell of Intense Heat, the lifespan of sentient beings is measured at half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) by calculation; only then do they pass away.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Constantly creating the causes of evil deeds, Yet longing for the fruits of peace and happiness,”
Separated from humans and devas, one shall be born in the Reviving Hell.
Those who strike or revile their teachers, parents, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas;
those with wrong views who sever their roots of goodness—these undergo great suffering in the Extremely Hot Hell.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The lifespan in that Great Avīci Hell is measured such that one dies after this [period]."

If Devadatta or any other deluded person conceives an evil mind toward the Tathāgata, destroys stūpas and monasteries, burns scriptures and images, sheds the blood of a Buddha, kills an Arhat, or subjects Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs to forced labor, they will, upon the end of their lives, inevitably fall into the Avīci Great Hell, where they shall suffer interminably.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who slander the teachings of the Three Vehicles, who kill noble Arhats, and who, out of folly,
disparage the pursuit of the Dharma, shall receive the retribution of the Avīci Hell."
"The fruit of the thorny bamboo destroys itself; Evil karma leads to birth in the evil realms.
Such is the fault of negligence: One shall suffer in the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, the lifespan is half a kalpa, after which one passes away.
Bhikṣus, you should know that in the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā, the lifespan is one kalpa, after which one passes away;
in the Heaven of Mahābrahmā, the lifespan is one and a half kalpas, after which one passes away."
Bhikṣus, you should know that in the Heaven of Limited Light, the lifespan is two kalpas before one passes away;
in the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, the lifespan is four kalpas before one passes away;
and in the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Light, the lifespan is eight kalpas before one passes away.
Bhikṣus, you should know that in the Heaven of Limited Tranquility, the lifespan is sixteen kalpas before one’s life ends;
in the Heaven of Immeasurable Tranquility, the lifespan is thirty-two kalpas before one’s life ends;
and in the Heaven of Universal Tranquility, the lifespan is sixty-four kalpas before one’s life ends.
Bhikṣus, you should know that the gods of the Cloudless Heaven have a lifespan of one hundred and twenty-five kalpas, after which they pass away;
the gods of the Heaven of Merit-Born have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty kalpas, after which they pass away;
and the gods of the Vast Fruit Heaven have a lifespan of five hundred kalpas, after which they pass away.
The lifespan in the Heaven of No Perception is likewise.
Bhikṣus, you should know that in the Heaven of No Affliction, the lifespan is one thousand kalpas, after which one passes away;
in the Heaven of No Heat, the lifespan is two thousand kalpas, after which one passes away.
Bhikṣus, you should know that in the Sudarśana Heaven the lifespan is four thousand kalpas, after which one’s life ends;
in the Sudṛśa Heaven the lifespan is eight thousand kalpas, after which one’s life ends;
and in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven the lifespan is sixteen thousand kalpas, after which one’s life ends.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that the lifespan of sentient beings in the Sphere of Infinite Space is twenty thousand great kalpas, after which they pass away;
in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the lifespan is forty thousand great kalpas, after which they pass away;
in the Sphere of Nothingness, the lifespan is sixty thousand great kalpas, after which they pass away.”
"The lifespan of sentient beings in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is eighty thousand great kalpas; only after that do they pass away.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In this way, from within the Avīci Great Hell up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, saṃsāra proceeds in such a manner."
Bhikṣus, you should know that sentient beings thus transmigrate through the five destinies without ceasing, manifesting the three characteristics of arising, change, and cessation.
"O Bhikṣus, you should know that these three natures of the revolving wheel are not to be delighted in nor envied even for a brief moment; they do not endure for even a single kṣaṇa."
Why is this? Bhikṣus, you should know that because it is of the nature of suffering, it is not to be cherished or delighted in.
This is true even of a small amount of impurity; how much more so of a great amount?
Such slight defilements are not to be delighted in, nor are they to be envied.
They last for but a single moment and are not ultimate. Why is this?
Bhikṣus, you should know that the suffering of saṃsāra is not to be relished.

If there are deluded and ignorant beings who wander through the five destinies without ceasing their coming and going, constantly failing to abandon the cycle of rebirth, they cannot escape the suffering within the hells, nor can they escape the suffering among the hungry ghosts; they perpetually fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus:
"One should not take delight in this great suffering of saṃsāra.
Bhikṣus, you should know that you must exert yourselves with diligence and vigor to sever and extinguish saṃsāra.
When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, those bhikṣus, with single-minded joy, believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
*The Sūtra on Measuring Life Spans Spoken by the Buddha*.
